questions_asked:
# Expert Question 1

The daily number of reported Wordle scores is not a steady stream: it spikes on
weekends and on easy days, and dips mid-week and on hard days.

When you look at how people actually share their Wordle results, does the number
of tweets you'd expect depend mostly on how hard that day's word was, or on
whether it was a weekend? Which one matters more to you in real life?

# Expert Question 2

You confirmed the weekly cycle is the primary driver of how many scores get
posted, and word attributes a secondary effect.

On hard days, people give up and don't post their loss. When a word is hard,
do you think fewer people post at all — or the same people post, just more of
them show a failed (X) result?

# Expert Question 3

You said the X share (failure rate) is the cleaner difficulty signal, and the
count drop is the weaker one.

When the NYT uses your model to plan a future puzzle, what size of error in
your predicted failure rate would make the prediction useless to them — too
wrong to act on? In other words, how close does your guess need to be for it
to be worth using?
expert_answers:
Weekend/day-of-week matters more, and it is the more reliable driver.

In real life, the dominant mechanism is routine: people post their grid as part of a daily social ritual, and that ritual is far more likely to happen when people have leisure time — weekends and holidays. That produces a large, highly regular weekly cycle that shows up regardless of the word.

Word difficulty is a real but secondary effect, and it works in both directions: an easy word produces more "got it in 2" brags (more posts), while a very hard word produces more failures, and people are somewhat less likely to post a loss — so hard days dampen volume. But this effect is smaller and noisier than the weekend effect, and it is partly confounded with it.

Empirical judgment: the weekly cycle typically accounts for a swing on the order of tens of percent in daily volume, whereas word-difficulty effects are usually a smaller fraction of that. So for explaining and predicting the count of reported results, treat day-of-week as the primary factor and word attributes as a secondary adjustment.

Fewer people post at all — the drop in volume is real, not just a redistribution of the same posters.

The mechanism is selective non-posting: people who fail are less likely to share than people who succeed, and this is well documented in Wordle-sharing behavior. So on a hard day, the marginal poster — someone who would have posted a "4/6" on an easy day — simply doesn't post when they bust. The result is both effects at once: total volume falls, and the X share among those who do post rises.

But the volume effect is the smaller and noisier of the two. The X-percentage shift is the more visible and more reliable signal of difficulty, because it is measured within the fixed pool of people who did post. The count drop is diluted by the many routine posters who post regardless of outcome.

Empirical judgment: on a hard day, expect a modest decline in total reported results (a few percent to low tens of percent) plus a clear rise in the X share. The X share is the cleaner difficulty indicator; the count is the weaker one.

For planning purposes, a predicted failure rate is useful if it is accurate to within roughly a few percentage points — call it about ±2 to ±3 percentage points on the X share.

Reason: the X share itself typically ranges from about 1–2% on easy words to roughly 10–20% on the hardest ones, with most days in the low single digits. An error of ±2–3 points is small relative to that spread, so it still separates an easy day from a hard day and supports a real decision (e.g., whether a puzzle is likely to frustrate players). Once the error approaches the size of the day-to-day spread itself — say ±5 points or more — the prediction can no longer distinguish a hard word from an easy one, and it stops being actionable.

This is an empirical judgment, not a precise figure.
